crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Course-specific AI tutors are AI systems built around a single course, its materials, objectives, assessments, and policies. They differ from general-purpose chatbots because their knowledge and behavior are bounded by the instructor's design. Common uses include answering student questions, giving hints on problem sets, explaining concepts from the course readings, and generating practice items. The site's library holds 135 research papers, and only a portion of that work addresses course-specific tutoring directly.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A course-specific tutor typically runs on a large language model as its base, with a retrieval layer over the course's own documents, lecture transcripts, problem sets, and rubrics. It may live inside a learning management system, a standalone web application, or a chat interface that students already use. The system needs an index of course materials, often a vector database, and a way to log interactions for review. Compute can be cloud-based or hosted on institutional servers, depending on privacy and cost requirements.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with instructors and course teams curating the knowledge base, writing system instructions, and setting boundaries for what the tutor may discuss. They test the tutor against common student questions, misconceptions, and edge cases before releasing it to a class. Many implementations use retrieval augmented generation so that answers point back to specific course sources rather than the open web. Evaluation often combines automated checks with human review of chat transcripts to catch errors and improve prompts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk start with the course materials themselves, which may be copyrighted, licensed, or subject to institutional rules about sharing. Student data privacy is a central concern, so logs and transcripts typically have clear retention and access policies. Provenance means tracking which sources an answer draws from and keeping a record that instructors and students can inspect. Tutors usually disclose that they are AI systems and not human instructors, and they generally avoid giving grades or definitive judgments without human review. Risks include hallucination, bias, over-reliance, and unequal access to the technology.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Course-specific tutors are likely to become more tightly integrated with learning management systems and assessment tools. More emphasis is expected on citation, source grounding, and transparent reasoning so that students can see where an answer comes from. Adaptive tutoring that responds to a student's progress data is an active area of development, though it raises new privacy questions. The site catalogues 732 AI tools, a sign of how crowded the general market is, while course-specific tutors remain a smaller and more tailored category.
